extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, policymakers, students and scholars of public opinion and mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting principles about how public opinion is formed and how media, stereotypes, attention, and audience characteristics shape perception and reporting; useful for designing or evaluating news and public communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of attention and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: We learn to understand why our addled minds seize so little with precision, why they are caught up and tossed about in a kind of tarantella by headlines and catch-words... Experiment shows that the speed, the accuracy, and the intellectual quality of association is deranged by what we are taught to call emotional conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages assuming limited attention span and variable speed/accuracy of mental association. Keep headlines and ledes clear and simple; recognize emotional conflicts can slow or distort comprehension. Anti-pattern: expecting detailed, reflective processing from rapid headline readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for audience emotional conflicts and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviously our public opinion is in intermittent contact with complexes of all sorts; with ambition and economic interest, personal animosity, racial prejudice, class feeling and what not. They distort our reading, our thinking, our talking and our behavior in a great variety of ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how content may interact with audience motives and prejudices. Test whether messaging activates partisanship, economic self-interest, or resentments that will distort reception. Example: propaganda tailored to economic interest will be received differently than neutral analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match psychic level (broad vs. narrow appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'broad appeal' takes account of the quality of association, and is made to those susceptibilities which are widely distributed. A 'narrow' or a 'special' appeal is one made to those susceptibilities which are uncommon. For the 'psychic level' on which the stimulus acts determines whether the public is to be potentially a large or a small one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing content, explicitly choose whether to address widely distributed sensibilities (simple, familiar cues) or specialized audiences (technical detail). Example: large-circulation magazines 'prefer the face of a pretty girl' because it hits a widely distributed level. Anti-pattern: using specialized jargon for a mass homepage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for limited literacy and impaired attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass of absolutely illiterate, of depressed, feeble-minded, grossly neurotic, undernourished and frustrated individuals, is very considerable... Thus a wide popular appeal is circulated among persons who are mentally children or barbarians... stopped by them in little eddies of misunderstanding, where it is discolored with prejudice and far fetched analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clarity, simple vocabulary, and strong visual cues for broad audiences; avoid reliance on long paragraphs or subtle argumentation when addressing mass public. Example: mass propaganda targets simplest susceptibilities. Scoring note: content aimed at a general homepage should be readable at low literacy levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes as perceptual shortcuts (economy of attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most facts in consciousness seem to be partly made... A report is the joint product of the knower and known... In the form stereotyping for many of our culture... our culture has taught us to perceive what we have picked out. In the form stereotyping, for many of our culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize stereotypes economize cognition by providing ready-made images and classifications; they save attention but risk distortion. Evaluate whether usage of stereotypes is deliberately simplifying for clarity or lazily substituting for factual reporting. Anti-pattern: letting stock images/labels replace reporting on actual facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of stereotype-driven fabrication and memory error
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus out of forty trained observers writing a responsible account of a scene that was just happened before their eyes, more than a majority saw a scene that had not taken place... They saw their stereotype of such a brawl.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify eyewitness and sourced claims; be skeptical of confident, detailed reports produced quickly. Use corroboration and records (photos, timestamps). Scoring: accounts that rely on single rapid eyewitnesses without corroboration should be downgraded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium matters: images have stronger, more immediate effects than words
rubrics_metrics.description: On the screen the whole process of observing, describing, reporting, and then imagining, has been accomplished for you... The shadowy idea becomes vivid; your hazy notion... takes vivid shape when you see the Birth of a Nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using imagery (photos, film) expect durable mental impressions and stronger persuasion than textual descriptions. Evaluate visual content for accuracy and potential to create lasting, possibly misleading, images. Anti-pattern: relying on a striking image to substitute for nuanced textual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural framing and Americanization changes perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Americanization, for example, is superficially at least the substitution of American for European stereotypes... This constitutes a change of mind... His eye sees differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how cultural frames and familiar national tropes shape interpretation. For multi-cultural audiences, test whether frames exclude or mischaracterize minorities. Example: pageants that dress immigrant groups into 'American' forms may conceal their original identities and foster assimilationist interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes serve as defenses of social order (resistance to challenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The systems of stereotypes may be the core of our personal tradition, the defenses of our position in society... Any disturbance of the stereotypes seems like an attack upon the foundations of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect audiences to resist reporting that threatens entrenched social narratives; anticipate defensive backlash. When evaluating controversial content, consider whether it challenges or reinforces social comforts and how that affects reception and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification is purpose-relative; prefer individualized reporting where dignity matters
rubrics_metrics.description: All classification is in relation to some purpose not necessarily our own... There is a taint on any contact between two people which does not affirm as an axiom the personal inviolability of both... Those whom we love and admire most are the men and women whose consciousness is peopled thickly with persons rather than with types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For intimate or human-centered stories, prioritize individualized, person-focused reporting over typifying labels. Scoring note: features that humanize subjects score higher on respectfulness and depth than those that reduce to stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filters and sources modify reports (joint product of knower and known)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the environment with which our public opinions deal is refracted in many ways, by censorship and privacy at the source, by physical and social barriers at the other end, by scanty attention, by the poverty of language, by distraction... These limitations upon our access... combine with the obscurity and complexity of the facts themselves to thwart clarity and justice of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate provenance: account for censorship, privacy constraints, social barriers, and the language available to sources. Be transparent about limits of access and how they might distort reporting. Anti-pattern: presenting filtered reports as full, objective accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation and circular reasoning via stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The stereotype is like the lavender window-panes on Beacon Street... It stamps itself upon the evidence in the very act of securing the evidence. That is why the accounts of returning travellers are often an interesting tale of what the traveller carried abroad with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against circular logic where expectations shape observations which are then treated as evidence. Use independent checks and seek disconfirming evidence. Scoring: reporting that fails to test stereotype-driven assumptions should be marked as lower reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/biographical tracing of ideas improves clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: What matters is the character of the stereotypes and the gullibility with which we employ them. And these in the end depend upon those inclusive patterns which constitute our philosophy of life... We tend... to realize more and more clearly when our ideas started, where they started, how they came to us, why we accepted them. All useful history is antiseptic in this fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims or narratives, include tracing of origins (schoolbooks, fairy tales, traditions) that produced prevailing stereotypes. This historical context helps decontaminate assumptions. Anti-pattern: presenting timeless or ahistorical assertions as self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate granularity: balance stereotype economy with need for detailed inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: There is economy in this. For the attempt to see all things freshly and in detail... an attentive curiosity is for most people, practically out of the question... What matters is the character of the stereotypes and the gullibility with which we employ them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose granularity appropriate to purpose: use stereotypes for quick orientation but invest in detailed inquiry where decisions or justice are at stake. Scoring guidance: shallow, stereotype-driven summaries are acceptable for fast overviews but score poorly for investigative depth.
